growth_story.headline: After a 2000s boom, Brazil's income per person grew just 0.6 percent a year from 2012, and only passed its 2013 high in 2024.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 Brazil's income per person has grown in three eras: 0.5 percent a year in 1990–2003, 3.4 in 2004–2011 and 0.6 in 2012–2025. The sources say little about the first era beyond waves of trade opening in the early 1990s and early 2000s. In the fast middle era, the OECD notes, a new middle class emerged amid strong growth. Productivity has been falling since about 2010, and a slump that the IMF notes came with falling commodity prices cut income per person by 4.3 percent in 2015 and 4.0 percent in 2016. After a 3.8 percent fall in 2020, a recovery driven by more jobs, household spending and government support lifted income per person past its 2013 high in 2024, to a new peak in 2025.

threads.title: Commodity prices and the 2015 slump
threads.text: Brazil's ups and downs have tracked the prices of what it sells abroad. The IMF notes that the deep downturn of 2015, when income per person fell 4.3 percent, followed by 4.0 percent in 2016, came as commodity prices fell.

threads.text: Productivity has been falling since 2010, the OECD finds, with low investment in roads and other infrastructure part of the reason. The World Bank still names low productivity, along with the budget imbalance, as a limit on faster growth in 2026.

threads.title: More workers, not more productivity
threads.text: Growth for decades has come mostly from a growing workforce, and the recent recovery came from more people in jobs, helped by household spending and government support. The OECD expects an ageing population to take back that boost over the next 25 years.

threads.text: Government debt is high and is financed at high interest rates. The extra cost of government borrowing spiked in the 2014–2016 crisis and rose again in 2024 amid doubts about the budget rules.

threads.text: Brazil has become the world's top soybean seller, mostly to China, and China now takes a far larger share of its exports than in the early 1990s. As commodities make up more of what Brazil sells, growth is more exposed to world prices.

since_last_year.text: Growth in income per person slowed from 3.0 percent in 2024 to 1.9 percent in 2025, as high interest rates aimed at inflation and less government support cooled demand, while strong soy harvests softened the slowdown. In 2026 the war in the Middle East pushed up world oil prices, bringing Brazil an income windfall as a net oil exporter. The central bank began cutting its policy rate in March 2026, and the newly ratified EU–Mercosur trade agreement is entering the implementation stage.

growth_story.tension: The sources call Brazil's recent growth remarkably resilient, and the data agree for 2022–2024, when income per person grew between 2.6 and 3.0 percent a year. Over the longer run the picture is weaker: income per person grew 0.9 percent a year in 2016–2025, against 1.9 in the decade before, and the 2025 peak sits only a little above the 2013 level.
